title: Not things, but judgments
hook: people are upset not by things but by their judgments about things (Enchiridion 5)
tomorrow: The horse is handsome, not you

segments.voice: Yesterday at the baths: two aims at every door, the errand and your purpose. Your line was and keep my purpose.

Two people are stuck in the same traffic jam, same lane, same minute. One is pounding the wheel, already rehearsing the apology to the boss. The other has turned up the radio and is singing badly. Same cars, same delay, same red brake lights stretching to the bridge. So what, exactly, is upsetting the first driver? If it were the traffic, it would be upsetting both of them. Section five of the handbook gives Epictetus' answer, and it fits in a single breath.
screen: `TWO DRIVERS, ONE JAM.` → `ONE FURIOUS, ONE SINGING.` → `WHAT'S DOING THE UPSETTING?`

segments.voice: In George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The Greek word for those opinions is dogmata, the plural of today's word. Today, dogma sounds like rigid doctrine, something you're not allowed to question. In Epictetus' Greek it's humbler. It comes from a verb meaning to seem: a dogma is what seems so to you, the verdict you've passed before you notice you passed it. The traffic is a thing. I'm going to be fired, this always happens to me: those are dogmata. His example: death isn't terrible, or it would have seemed so to Socrates, who faced his own calmly. The terrible part is the judgment that death is terrible. You can disagree with him about death and still try the move on a parking ticket. Then he adds a ladder. An untrained person blames others when things go badly; someone starting out blames themself; someone trained blames neither. The sentence has a long echo. The novelist Laurence Sterne put it, in Greek, at the front of Tristram Shandy. In the twentieth century the psychologist Albert Ellis named Epictetus as an influence on his therapy, which taught people to catch the belief that sits between an event and the feeling. Here is the honest limit. Epictetus isn't saying pain is imaginary or that nothing out there is wrong. He's saying the part that churns inside is built partly from our own verdicts. And a verdict can be looked at again.
screen: `NOT THE THINGS, BUT THE OPINIONS.` · `DOGMA: WHAT SEEMS SO TO ME.` · `SOCRATES, AND THE LADDER OF BLAME.` · `FROM STERNE TO THE THERAPY ROOM.` · then, large: `IT'S MY VIEW.`

segments.voice: Bring back one small thing that upset you this week, a text, a delay, a look, and first describe only what a camera would see: he replied with one word; the train came twelve minutes late. Then find the judgment underneath, he's annoyed with me, my whole day is ruined, and add plainly: it's my view. Don't argue with it yet; just see that it's a view, sitting there.
Dogma. In Epictetus' Greek, not rigid doctrine but a judgment, what seems so to you. It's our dogmata, he says, that disturb us. Today's word.
Your line: it's my view. What happened is one thing; what I say about it is another. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 337 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HORSE IS HANDSOME, NOT YOU.`

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often separate what happened from the judgment they've added to it, sometimes writing the two side by side.

chat.says: What did Epictetus mean about things not upsetting us?
options: We're disturbed by our judgments about what happens, not the events themselves.
That bad things don't truly happen, and pain is all in your head.
That if you stay calm, nothing bad will ever happen to you.
chat.meaning: Section five: people are disturbed not by things but by their opinions about them. Pain is real; the churn is partly our own verdicts.
